languages.title: Python -- Language Reference
languages.subtitle: Interpreted, garbage-collected, dynamically typed. Great for beginners and data work. Slow for CPU-heavy tasks.

rows.label: Compiled or Interpreted
rows.helpText: Python compiles your .py to bytecode (.pyc), then the CPython interpreter reads it instruction by instruction. It never becomes native machine code unless you use tools like Nuitka or Cython.

rows.label: Execution Speed
rows.helpText: Python is 10-100x slower than C for pure computation. The GIL, dynamic typing, and interpretation all contribute. Fine for I/O, scripting, and glue code.

rows.label: Startup Time
rows.helpText: Python loads the interpreter, imports modules, compiles bytecode. Heavier than C but lighter than Java.

rows.label: Memory Model
rows.helpText: Python uses reference counting plus a cyclic garbage collector. You never call malloc or free. Objects are freed when nothing references them.

rows.label: Manual Memory Control
rows.helpText: You cannot control when memory is allocated or freed. Python decides. This prevents memory leaks from programmer error but means you can't optimize memory usage.

rows.label: Stack vs Heap
rows.helpText: All Python objects live on the heap. Local variables are references (pointers) to heap objects. The stack only holds these references, not the data itself.

rows.label: True Parallelism
rows.helpText: The Global Interpreter Lock means only one thread executes Python at a time. For CPU parallelism, use multiprocessing (separate processes) or C extensions.

rows.label: Async/Await
rows.helpText: Python has native async/await for I/O concurrency. Good for network requests, file I/O, web servers. Not for CPU-bound work.

rows.label: Threads
rows.helpText: threading module exists but threads don't run in parallel for Python code due to the GIL. Useful only for I/O-bound waiting.

rows.label: Classes
rows.helpText: Full class support with constructors (__init__), methods, properties, class variables, static methods.

rows.label: Inheritance
rows.helpText: Python supports multiple inheritance with MRO (Method Resolution Order). Can inherit from multiple classes.

rows.label: Polymorphism
rows.helpText: If it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, it's a duck. No interfaces needed -- just implement the same methods.

rows.label: Interfaces
rows.helpText: Python has Abstract Base Classes (abc module) but no formal interface keyword. Duck typing is the standard approach.

rows.label: Encapsulation
rows.helpText: Python uses _ prefix for 'private' but nothing is truly private. It's a convention, not enforced by the language.

rows.label: Static Types
rows.helpText: Python is dynamically typed. Type hints (PEP 484) exist but are not enforced at runtime -- they're for tools like mypy.

rows.label: Generics
rows.helpText: Generic type hints exist (list[int], dict[str, Any]) but are not enforced. The runtime doesn't check them.

rows.label: Null Safety
rows.helpText: None can be assigned to anything. No compile-time null checks. NoneType errors are a top Python bug.

rows.label: Mutable Default Args
rows.helpText: def f(items=[]): -- the default list is shared across ALL calls. A classic Python trap. Use None as default instead.

rows.label: Indentation is Syntax
rows.helpText: Python uses indentation to define blocks. No braces. A misaligned line changes the program's meaning.

rows.label: GIL
rows.helpText: The Global Interpreter Lock is Python's biggest architectural constraint. It prevents true multi-threaded parallelism for CPU work.

languages.title: C -- Language Reference
languages.subtitle: Compiled to native code. Manual memory. Maximum control, maximum responsibility. The language that built operating systems.

rows.label: Compiled or Interpreted
rows.helpText: C compiles directly to machine code. No interpreter, no VM, no runtime. The output is a standalone binary the CPU executes directly.

rows.label: Execution Speed
rows.helpText: C code runs at near-hardware speed. No overhead from garbage collection, interpretation, or dynamic dispatch. This is why OS kernels are written in C.

rows.label: Startup Time
rows.helpText: A C binary starts immediately. No runtime to load, no bytecode to compile, no modules to import.

rows.label: Memory Model
rows.helpText: You allocate memory with malloc() and free it with free(). Forget to free = memory leak. Free twice = crash. Free then use = undefined behavior.

rows.label: Stack vs Heap
rows.helpText: Local variables go on the stack (automatic, fast, limited size). Dynamic data goes on the heap (malloc, unlimited, you manage lifetime). Understanding this distinction is critical in C.

rows.label: Pointers
rows.helpText: Pointers are memory addresses. C gives you direct access to memory through pointers. Powerful but dangerous -- invalid pointers cause segfaults and security vulnerabilities.

rows.label: Buffer Overflows
rows.helpText: C does not check array bounds. Writing past the end of an array overwrites whatever is next in memory. This is the #1 source of security vulnerabilities in C code.

rows.label: True Parallelism
rows.helpText: C threads run truly in parallel on multiple CPU cores. No GIL. But you must handle synchronization (mutexes, race conditions) yourself.

rows.label: Async/Await
rows.helpText: C has no built-in async. You can use libraries like libuv or write event loops manually, but it's not a language feature.

rows.label: Data Races
rows.helpText: C does nothing to prevent two threads from writing to the same memory simultaneously. You must use mutexes and atomics correctly. Getting this wrong causes hard-to-debug crashes.

rows.label: Classes
rows.helpText: C has no classes. You use structs for data grouping and function pointers for behavior. It's manual but possible.

rows.label: Inheritance
rows.helpText: No language support. You can simulate it by embedding one struct inside another, but the compiler doesn't help you.

rows.label: Polymorphism
rows.helpText: You can create vtable-like dispatch using arrays of function pointers, but it's entirely manual. No compiler support.

rows.label: Interfaces
rows.helpText: No concept of interfaces. You use conventions and function pointer structs.

rows.label: Encapsulation
rows.helpText: You can hide implementation in .c files and only expose declarations in .h headers. But anything in a struct is accessible.

rows.label: Static Types
rows.helpText: C is statically typed. Every variable has a declared type checked at compile time.

rows.label: Generics
rows.helpText: C has no generics. You use void* (type-erased pointers) or preprocessor macros, both losing type safety.

rows.label: Null Safety
rows.helpText: NULL can be assigned to any pointer. Dereferencing NULL = crash (segfault). No compile-time protection.

rows.label: Undefined Behavior
rows.helpText: C has hundreds of undefined behaviors -- signed overflow, null deref, use-after-free, buffer overflow. The compiler assumes these never happen and optimizes accordingly.

rows.label: No Strings
rows.helpText: C has no string type. Strings are null-terminated char arrays. You manage the memory, the length, and the null terminator yourself.

rows.label: Header Files
rows.helpText: C separates declarations (.h) from implementations (.c). You must manually keep them in sync. Forgetting an include causes cryptic errors.

rows.label: Preprocessor
rows.helpText: #define macros are text substitution before compilation. They don't respect scope, types, or namespaces. Misuse causes baffling bugs.

languages.title: UniLogic -- Language Reference
languages.subtitle: Compiled, configurable runtime, multi-target. Python's ease with C's output. Everything is tunable.

rows.label: Compiled or Interpreted
rows.helpText: UL compiles to C (native binary), Python, JavaScript, WASM, or bytecode from the same source. You choose the target.

rows.label: Execution Speed
rows.helpText: When compiled to C -> native binary, UL code runs at the same speed as hand-written C. Other targets run at their platform's speed.

rows.label: Memory Model
rows.helpText: gc, manual, refcount, or arena -- all from one @dr line. Switch and recompile to see the difference. No other language lets you do this.

rows.label: Garbage Collection
rows.helpText: Using Boehm GC linked into the native binary. Automatic, no free() calls needed.

rows.label: Manual Memory
rows.helpText: memtake/memgive (malloc/free). You control allocation and deallocation.

rows.label: Reference Counting
rows.helpText: Automatic increment/decrement. Freed when count hits zero.

rows.label: Arena Allocation
rows.helpText: Bulk allocate, free everything at once. Fast for batch processing.

rows.label: True Parallelism
rows.helpText: pthreads when targeting C. Real OS threads, true parallelism.

rows.label: Data Parallelism
rows.helpText: OpenMP-based parallel for loops. Automatic work distribution.

rows.label: Async/Await
rows.helpText: Coroutine-based async. Non-blocking I/O.

rows.label: Cooperative
rows.helpText: Manual yield_now/schedule. Lightweight green threads.

rows.label: Types (structs)
rows.helpText: Zero-overhead C structs. Data only, no methods.

rows.label: Objects (OOP)
rows.helpText: Full OOP with constructors, methods, vtable-based polymorphism.

rows.label: Inheritance
rows.helpText: object Dog forks Animal -- copies and extends. Multiple inheritance supported.

rows.label: Polymorphism
rows.helpText: Variable typed as parent, assigned child -- vtable dispatches correctly.

rows.label: Interfaces
rows.helpText: interface keyword. Semcheck enforces all methods present.

rows.label: Static Types
rows.helpText: Full compile-time type checking in strict mode.

rows.label: Dynamic Types
rows.helpText: Runtime type checking in dynamic mode. Switch with one @dr line.

rows.label: Gradual Types
rows.helpText: Mix typed and untyped. Typed where you want safety, untyped where you want speed.

rows.label: Null Safety
rows.helpText: @nullable annotation. Non-nullable by default.

main.py.annotated_code:
# function returning float -- calculates total cost of a list of prices with tax applied
# accepts: list of prices, optional tax rate (defaults to 10%)
def calculate_total(prices, tax_rate=0.10):
    """Calculate total price with tax."""
    # guard clause -- returns 0 immediately if the price list is empty, prevents errors downstream
    if not prices:
        return 0.0

    # accumulator variable -- will hold the running sum of all prices
    subtotal = 0
    # loop through every item in the list by index -- adds each price to the running total
    for i in range(len(prices)):
        subtotal += prices[i]

    # applies tax by multiplying subtotal by (1 + rate), e.g. 1.10 for 10% tax
    total = subtotal * (1 + tax_rate)
    # rounds to 2 decimal places to avoid floating point artifacts like 50.038999...
    return round(total, 2)


# entry point -- called when script runs directly, sets up test data and prints results
def main():
    # test data -- five price values to sum
    items = [12.99, 5.50, 3.75, 8.00, 15.25]
    # calls calculate_total with default 10% tax
    total = calculate_total(items)
    # output -- sum() is a builtin that adds list elements, :.2f formats to 2 decimal places
    print(f"Subtotal: ${sum(items):.2f}")
    print(f"Total with tax: ${total:.2f}")
    # len() returns the number of items in the list
    print(f"Items: {len(items)}")


# Python idiom -- only runs main() if this file is executed directly, not when imported
if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
